name: Sodium beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB salts)
lead: Sodium beta-hydroxybutyrate is a salt form of beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), the main ketone body the liver makes during fasting, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate diets. [1][2] In supplements, BHB is bound to sodium, potassium, magnesium or calcium; most products are racemic, so only about half is the biologically used D form. [3]
Sellers market ketone salts as a way to raise blood ketones without dietary restriction, with claims about appetite, energy and fat loss. [3] These claims are commonly discussed in fat-loss contexts.
Human studies of BHB administration are mostly small physiology trials in healthy people and in patients with diabetes or heart failure; none tests BHB salts for fat loss or appearance.

The appearance case for ketone salts is leanness: people use them alongside ketogenic or low-carbohydrate diets in the hope of easier adherence, appetite control and training energy while cutting body fat, and a few sports supplements pair them with caffeine as a pre-workout.[3][16] The human studies that exist are small, and the strongest relevant one examined blood ketone patterns during a six-week hypocaloric ketogenic diet rather than fat loss as an outcome.[14]

paras: Ketone bodies are produced by the liver and used by tissues when glucose is scarce; the two main ones are acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate. [2] Classic studies showed that during prolonged starvation the brain uses ketone bodies in place of much of its glucose. [4][5] Reviews have discussed ketone bodies in ketogenic diets, insulin resistance and mitochondrial metabolism. [6]
Salts slightly raise blood pH, whereas esters lower it, according to Wikipedia. [3] The most-studied ester is a separate compound, described in its own entry.

Wikipedia describes ketone salts as BHB bound to sodium, potassium, magnesium or calcium, usually in a racemic mix where only half is the usable D form, so a given rise in blood D-BHB comes with a larger mineral load.[3] In the study Wikipedia cites, esters produced higher blood D-BHB (about 2.8 mM) than salts (about 1.0 mM).[3] The main ester is a monoester of D-BHB and R-1,3-butanediol developed at the NIH by Richard Veech and Todd King, and later sold by several companies.[3] Wikipedia also reports that one ketone ester drink lowered ghrelin, the hunger hormone, and that exogenous ketones lower blood glucose by limiting liver glucose output and increasing uptake in peripheral tissue.[3]

Registered studies of exogenous ketosis include safety and tolerability of free BHB, effects on kidney function, cognition during exercise-heat stress, brain ketone metabolism in type 1 diabetes, a BHB ester in ALS, BHB in type 1 and type 2 diabetes, and nutritional ketosis in heart failure. [7][8][9][10][11][12][13] Several of these use esters or free BHB rather than salts. No studies found testing sodium BHB salts specifically for fat loss or appearance.

A randomized trial in Clinical Nutrition ESPEN (2023) fed non-diabetic adults with overweight or obesity a hypocaloric ketogenic diet for six weeks, with two daily servings of racemic ketone salt (6 g R-BHB plus 6 g S-BHB) or placebo, and compared blood ketone and glucose patterns; the authors framed it as the first look at sustained rather than single-dose use, noting that single doses transiently raise BHB by about 1 mM for one to two hours.[14]

In a physiology study of 10 healthy men, sodium BHB infused into one leg artery raised local venous BHB to about 3.4 mM versus 1.9 mM in the saline leg, but the researchers did not observe a direct effect on muscle protein turnover under those conditions.[15] A randomized crossover trial in 24 recreationally active adults tested a pre-workout containing about 7 g of BHB salts with caffeine and amino acids; the authors reported improved high-intensity cycling performance in both keto-naive and keto-adapted participants.[16]
The European Food Safety Authority published a 2022 scientific opinion on the safety of beta-hydroxybutyrate salts as a novel food.[17]

card.summary: Ketone-salt supplements raise blood BHB; fat-loss and looks claims have not been tested.
card.note: Sodium load; many products are racemic.

quick.overview:
BHB salts are supplements that bind the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate to minerals such as sodium. They are sold to raise blood ketones without fasting or a ketogenic diet.

Research is limited to small physiology studies, and fat loss from the salts has not been shown in published trials found here.
quick.mechanism: BHB is a fuel the body makes during fasting and uses in the brain and muscle. Salts supply it directly, though racemic products contain a form that is less used.
quick.risks: Salts add a mineral load (such as sodium) and slightly raise blood pH. Long-term safety data in healthy dieters are limited.
